segments.text: Light travels along a silicon wire, a waveguide, and we want to split it evenly into two.
A person would draw a smooth fork. Squeezed into this small box, it delivers only 86% of the light.
A computer drew this instead: a strange, organic pattern in the same box. It delivers 99.8%.
How does a computer invent shapes no human would draw?
The trick is to run light backward. It's called the adjoint method.
First, turn design into numbers: each pixel of the box gets a value p, from 0 for glass to 1 for silicon.
A merit, F(p), scores the device: the fraction of light that reaches the two outputs.
Picture F as a landscape over all possible designs. To improve, walk uphill, along the gradient.
The obvious way to find it: nudge one pixel, rerun the whole simulation, and see how F changes.
That's one simulation per pixel: four thousand for this little box, and millions for a metalens.
With a million pixels and a minute per simulation, one step uphill would take two years.
Here's the way out. At one frequency, a wave simulation on a grid is one big linear system: A x = b.
b is the source, x is the field everywhere, and the matrix A holds the material, so it depends on p.
Differentiate both sides with respect to one pixel, and solve for how the field changes.
The merit's slope becomes a chain of three factors: a row, the inverse of A, and one column per pixel.
Multiply right to left, and every column costs a solve with A: one simulation per pixel, again.
But multiply left to right! The row times A⁻¹ is a single vector, λ, and it takes just one extra solve.
Then each pixel's slope is a cheap product: two simulations give the whole gradient, however many pixels there are.
So what is λ, physically? Light obeys reciprocity: swap a source and a detector, and the signal stays the same.
In matrix terms, Aᵀ = A. So λ comes from the same simulation, with the source moved to the outputs: light sent backward.
Nudge one pixel, and it scatters a tiny wavelet, with a strength set by the forward light hitting it.
The backward field there tells how that wavelet reaches the outputs, and whether it arrives in step with the light already there.
So each pixel's slope is the forward field times the adjoint field: the sensitivity map, for every pixel at once.
Update every pixel, simulate again, and repeat. Watch the device take shape.
Light run backward tells every pixel what to do.
You don't even need to derive adjoints by hand. Take a phase mask, then episode one's free-space propagation.
It's a chain: multiply by the mask, FFT, multiply by the transfer function H, inverse FFT, then square.
Automatic differentiation, the engine of deep learning, runs the chain backward: FFTs become inverse FFTs, and H becomes its conjugate.
For propagating waves, conjugating H just flips the sign of z. The backward pass really does send light backward.
Now gradient descent shapes the mask to project any picture. Watch the image sharpen as the error falls.
Episode five's Gerchberg–Saxton loop was a clever heuristic; gradients make it an optimization with any goal.
Now go further: design the optics and the software together.
A camera records a scene through our optics, adding noise; then an algorithm, here episode three's Wiener filter, sharpens it.
Compare the result with the truth, and send the gradient back through everything: the filter, the noise, the light, into the optics.
Ask for sharp images at every depth. An ordinary lens is sharp only in focus; elsewhere, its point-spread function, the PSF, blurs.
The learned optics gives up a perfect focus for a PSF that hardly changes with depth, which the filter can undo everywhere.
In code, it's a three-line loop: simulate, take the gradient, step, a few hundred times.
Real devices add rules: each pixel must be all silicon or all glass, with no feature too small to fabricate.
The landscape has many hills, so different starting guesses climb to different designs: all good, none guaranteed best.
And the optimizer exploits every error in its model: this lens shines in a cheap simulation, but loses half its light in a careful one.
So inverse design needs models fast enough to run thousands of times, and accurate enough to trust.
One forward and one backward simulation give the gradient for every pixel at once.
And that completes our season: plane waves, lenses as Fourier transforms, the diffraction limit, coherence, phase, flat optics, periodic structures, trapped light, Maxwell on a grid, and design.
Ten ideas, one thread.
Light is linear: in the right basis, the physics is simple; run it backward, and the design is too.
